items.title: FBI arrests OpenAI employee accused of placing recording device in company conference room
items.description: An OpenAI engineer has been charged with installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said was a bid to capture conversations about the firm’s technology.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Attendees gather at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2026. (Jeff Chiu / AP Photo)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jeff Chiu</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: An OpenAI engineer has been charged with installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said was a bid to capture conversations about the firm’s technology.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.

The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden in the conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.

The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications, but the company said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio monitoring capabilities. OpenAI said it had evidence the employee planned to place other listening devices throughout other parts of the office building for the purpose of recording meetings.

“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.

Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. He is due back in court on Oct. 19.

The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to the complaint

Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a camera at the time it was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on a half-dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space, the complaint says.

The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device was installed, according to the FBI.

The complaint also he also used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

Days before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left behind an unattended bag in a different room that, when opened by OpenAI personnel, was found to contain his wallet, identification and another recording device similar to the one placed in the conference room.

Eric Tucker, The Associated Press

items.title: An Atlantic Canadian business was hit by U.S. tariffs. They responded by doing this
items.description: An Island trailer manufacturer is shifting its focus to Canadian customers as U.S. tariffs have disrupted its plans for growth.

items._ogDesc: An Island trailer manufacturer is shifting its focus to Canadian customers as U.S. tariffs have disrupted its plans for growth.
items.body:
COLEMAN, P.E.I. – An Island trailer manufacturer is shifting its focus to Canadian customers as U.S. tariffs have disrupted its plans for growth.

Trout River Industries has struggled since the trade war began, says president Stephen Kennaugh. It has absorbed nearly $1 million in tariff costs, while sales have fallen on both sides of the border.

“We’re survivors. So, we’re going to survive anyway,” Kennaugh said. “We have 106 people here and they all have paycheques, they all have mortgages and they all have groceries. We’re responsible for that.”

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The U.S. once accounted for 40 per cent of Trout River’s sales, with the company pushing for more. Now, every trailer it sells south of the border faces a 25 per cent tariff. The company bears half that cost, while American dealerships and customers cover the rest. Uncertainty is also making it difficult to plan with partners.

The manufacturer builds large commercial trailers that use a conveyor belt to unload cargo, rather than tipping up like a dump trailer. They’re particularly popular in the paving industry, though the trailers are also used in agriculture.

Trout River is one of 17 Island businesses and organizations awarded non-repayable funding from Ottawa this month through the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. They’re sharing more than $6.9 million to help them respond to U.S. tariffs.

A grant of nearly $988,000 will help Trout River pay for a newly completed inventory building, which will allow workers to prepare kits containing all the parts needed for each trailer, so everything arrives together when production begins. Better inventory control will also allow the company to keep less stock on hand.

“The efficiency and the cost saving is going to help us to compete,” Kennaugh said.

Across the industry, the trade war has taught manufacturers some hard lessons, says Ron Marcolin, the divisional vice-president for New Brunswick and P.E.I. with Canadian Manufacturers and Exporters.

“We can’t count on the United States going forward, exclusively. And some companies did that for a number of years,” he said. “Diversification is key.”

That rings true on Trout River’s factory floor. Kennaugh still wants to sell as many trailers as possible in the U.S., but hopes growth at home will make those exports a smaller share of the business.

In Western Canada, the company is targeting the woodchip and fuel industries with a new trailer design. It’s also exploring tougher models for mines in northern Ontario.

But businesses in the region are also looking across the Atlantic Ocean for opportunity. Marcolin says manufacturers are “jumping at the chance” to export to Europe.

“We do have a strategic advantage on this coast,” he said.

Citing relatively few language barriers, straightforward currency exchanges and Canada’s reputation for quality and timely delivery, Marcolin is optimistic those efforts will be successful.

items._ogDesc: More than 200 saunas are being recalled in Canada due to a defective bench.
items.body:
More than 200 saunas are being recalled in Canada due to a defective bench.

Sauna360 issued a recall for its Tylö Halmstad and Kiruna Hybrid Saunas, Health Canada announced in a consumer product recall published Tuesday.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

“The saunas contain a bench that can collapse, posing a fall hazard to consumers,” Health Canada said.

According to Sauna360, based in Cokato, Minn., 246 affected saunas were sold in Canada between February 2025 and July 2026.

“Consumers should immediately stop using the recalled product and contact Sauna360 to schedule a free repair by a professional installer to retrofit the benches with additional hardware and supports,” Health Canada said in its advisory.

The following are the affected products and their serial numbers:

  • IS, Tylö Kiruna Hybrid™ 2, W/BLISS, 15A, 120V, LOW EMR, CB20-1, V1 (CSFxxABISxxTL-V1-4674 through CSFxxABADISxxTL-V1-18503)
  • IS, Tylö Kiruna Hybrid™ 2, W/BLISS, 20A, 120V, LOW EMR, CB20-1, V1 (CSFxxABISxxTL-V1-4674 through CSFxxABADISxxTL-V1-18503)
  • IS, Tylö Kiruna Hybrid™ 3, W/BLISS, 240V, LOW EMR, CB22-1, V1 (CSFxxABISxxTL-V1-4674 through CSFxxABADISxxTL-V1-18503)
  • TRAD, Tylö Halmstad™ 2, W/BLISS, 15A, 120V, CB21-1, V1 (CSFxxABTRxx-V1-4296 through CSFxxABADTRxx-V1-18577)
  • TRAD, Tylö Halmstad™ 2, W/BLISS, 20A, 120V, CB21-1, V1 (CSFxxABTRxx-V1-4296 through CSFxxABADTRxx-V1-18577)
  • TRAD, Tylö Halmstad™ 3, W/BLISS, 240V, CB23-1, V1 (SFxxABTRxx-V1-48413 through SFxxABTRxx-V1-48444)
  • TRAD, Tylö Halmstad™ 4, W/BLISS, 240V, CB23-1, V1 (SFxxABTRxx-V1-48413 through SFxxABTRxx-V1-48444)

As of Oct. 5, the company received nine reports of incidents, but there were no reports of injuries. The products were made in China.

Consumers are advised to call Sauna360 at 1-866-936-5962, or email recall@sauna360.com for more information.

Similar recall issued in September

The measure comes on the heels of a recall by the same manufacturer last month in both Canada and the United States.

Health Canada posted a consumer product recall notice in September for Sauna360’s Finnleo, Tylo, Polar, Radiant Health, and Helo brand saunas and infrared kits due to a “fire and burn hazard.”

The joint recall involved Health Canada, the United States Consumer Product Safety Commission and Sauna360. According to the notice, more than 48,000 units were sold between the two countries.

items.title: Millions of pink salmon are returning to spawn on Canada’s West Coast. But why?
items.description: Millions more of a species of salmon are returning to spawn up the Fraser River on Canada’s West Coast, but exactly why remains hotly disputed and solving that puzzle could have major implications for wild salmon stocks and coastal communities.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Atlantic salmon swim in the open net pens at a MOWI Canada West fish farm near Port Hardy, B.C. The image was supplied by MOWI Canada West.]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Millions more of a species of salmon are returning to spawn up the Fraser River on Canada’s West Coast, but exactly why remains hotly disputed and solving that puzzle could have major implications for wild salmon stocks and coastal communities.
items.body:
PORT HARDY, B.C. -- Millions more of a species of salmon are returning to spawn up the Fraser River on Canada’s West Coast, but exactly why remains hotly disputed, and the answer could have major implications for wild salmon stocks and coastal communities.

Some First Nations, in concert with environmental groups, have attributed this surge to the shutdown of dozens of salmon farms and are urging the federal government to enact a promised ban of the remainder of those farms by 2029.

But a W5 investigation has revealed a confidential internal assessment where federal government scientists say salmon farming operations pose a “minimal risk” to wild stocks and recommended reopening some of them, as the government itself is not outwardly committing to that ban.

“Farm presence (or absence) is only one of many variables, and current evidence does not demonstrate a causal link,” the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) said in a statement to W5, as another scientist suggested that surging salmon species, the pink salmon, may simply be doing better than other species in warming oceans.

A lot hinges on getting the science right: coastal communities are bracing for the impact of more salmon farm closures that could shed hundreds more jobs in what was once a billion-dollar industry, affect a valued way of life for First Nations, and change what Canadian consumers put on their plates.

The Discovery Islands: a pink salmon surge

Aboard his motorboat in the waters off the Discovery Islands, about 200 km northwest of Vancouver between Vancouver Island and the B.C. mainland, researcher Jody Erickson says he has noticed something incredible.

A seine net dropped from his motorboat can catch hundreds of young salmon smolts at a time, and Erickson draws up a few of them in a clear plastic case to see several different species: pink, chum and Chinook.

“What I would call very happy and healthy-looking fish right now,” he said. “No lice.”

It’s a far cry from what Erickson says he used to see in these waters a decade ago: juvenile salmon laden with parasites sticking to their skin, Erickson said. He still carries with him samples from those days that show small fish pockmarked with the parasites.

“They’re dying near fish farms. That’s what I see,” he said.

The Discovery Islands are a crucial thoroughfare for young salmon, who breed far up the freshwater rivers on B.C.’s coast, including the Fraser River, and then swim through these waters, around Vancouver Island, before making it out to sea.

Those islands, and the salmon farms that used to be there, were singled out by the Cohen Commission, a judicial inquiry that was called in 2009 after a salmon stock collapse.

Cohen pointed to many stressors that could affect the health of B.C. salmon, including warming waters, and recommended closing salmon farms in the Discovery Islands unless the federal fisheries minister is satisfied those farms pose at most a minimal risk to migrating sockeye salmon.

In 2019, the federal government followed through, refusing dozens of licences around the Discovery Islands, and then from the nearby Broughton Archipelago as a precaution. About half of all B.C. salmon farms are now gone.

A study by the Salmon Coast Field Station concluded that numbers of one species of lice dropped in the area once the salmon farms were removed, which could mean more salmon survive the long journey out to sea, said Research Crew Lead Kate Medcalf.

“As they out-migrate in these small sizes, they’re incredibly, incredibly vulnerable to parasitism and other stressors in the environment,” Medcalf said.

Erickson believes he is seeing the results of having fewer lice in the strait now.

“It’s very hopeful, because it shows that if we remove the fish farms, the fish can come back, really, really remarkably fast, faster than even I would have thought,” Erickson said.

Shuttered farms: the human cost

Nearby where Erickson cast his nets are what remains of several salmon farming operations. Some of them have been converted to other uses, while some have left no trace.

Those shutdowns meant lost jobs, and a narrowed future for the workers who hoped to launch long-term careers, said Kaitlin Guitard, a lab manager for one farm company, Mowi Canada West.

In an interview on the dock of one of the remaining farms, in the Queen Charlotte Strait near Port Hardy, she said she has lost hundreds of co-workers.

“It’s awful, it really is,” Guitard said. “I was relocated. But I think the hardest part for me was a lot of people that I worked with had either been laid off or could not wait around for certainty and had left.”

Guitard is among those fighting for the future of these farms, saying Canada needs the jobs and the food those farms produced.

Mowi Canada West’s production dropped from 40,000 tonnes a year, before the farms started to be removed in 2019, to 20,000 tonnes a year.

“The impact has been fairly devastating to the industry. We’ve lost 45 per cent of our production,” said Brian Kingzett, of the B.C. Salmon Farmers Association.

Kingzett says he’s aware that some farms have lice outbreaks, and that they do their best to manage them. But he doesn’t buy the connection drawn by researchers between his farms and the salmon collapse.

“We’ve had nine significant studies that have all identified that we can coexist with wild salmon, and we are continuing to innovate to further reduce any potential risks,” he said.

Rising numbers for salmon species; others are falling

Kingzett points to tracking by the Pacific Salmon Commission, a regulatory body run jointly by the Canadian and United States governments.

They use underwater sound waves and sonar to estimate the number of salmon passing the Mission hydroacoustic station in Mission, B.C., as they head up the Fraser River.

According to the commission figures, the number of pink salmon, which has a two-year life cycle, has doubled since 2019, from about 8.5 million to 17.7 million in 2025.

But the picture for another species of salmon, which has a four-year life cycle, is much less clear.

Promising returns of 8.1 million sockeye passing its station in 2025 were followed by disappointing returns under 3 million in 2026.

That figure was lower than 2022, when the Discovery Islands farms had been removed, and lower than in 2018 and 2014, when all the salmon farms were operating.

The DFO also monitors salmon escapement numbers by region along the coast. In region 13, which includes the Discovery Islands, coho and pink salmon are increasing, but chinook and sockeye salmon are not.

The connection between salmon farms and the health of wild stocks was also doubted by the DFO, which advised the fisheries minister in 2023 that its preferred option was to re-licence all 15 salmon farms in the Discovery Islands.

“Current Departmental science advice includes nine risk assessments that were completed specifically to advise the Department on the issue of licencing in the Discovery Islands, found that pathogen transmission from Atlantic salmon farms in the Discovery Islands poses minimal risk to Fraser River sockeye salmon population abundance and diversity under existing fish health management practices,” the department wrote.

The licenses were not re-issued. In 2024, the federal government proposed a draft transition plan that would ban open net pen salmon farming by 2029.

However, there has been no final transition plan released since.

In response to questions from CTV News about whether the federal government plans to follow through with the 2029 ban, a statement from Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson didn’t mention it.

“Pacific salmon are iconic to the West Coast and protecting and rebuilding wild salmon populations is a priority for our government,” the statement said, pointing to investments the government has made in three new salmon hatcheries, and consultation with stakeholders in B.C. this summer.

“There is no single solution to the challenges facing wild Pacific salmon, which is why we are taking a comprehensive approach to protecting and rebuilding these stocks,” she said.

Another school of thought

In his home in Nanaimo, B.C., retired fish scientist and winner of the Order of Canada Dick Beamish is convinced the answer to the mystery of the salmon returns lies farther out in the Pacific Ocean.

He points to studies that show pink salmon are surging not just in B.C. but worldwide, because they are better able to handle warming ocean temperatures.

“There will be populations in the north Pacific that are adapting to the ocean warming conditions better than others,” Beamish said in an interview.

Some species are coming back from their time in the ocean much smaller, on average, than in previous years, he said.

“What is probably happening with the warming that we’re seeing in the ocean is that there’s less food being produced that’s allowing salmon to accumulate the energy that they need to survive ocean winters,” Beamish said.

“That’s just a hypothesis. What we really need is scientific studies that are going to take a look at how this ocean warming is changing the overall food availability for salmon once they get into the open ocean,” he said.

Raising salmon on land?

Environmental groups are convinced that salmon farms are a threat and are pushing for alternatives to raise salmon on land.

In Port McNeill, in a cavernous warehouse only about a kilometre from where the Nimpkish River flows into the Queen Charlotte Strait, there are fish who will never see the ocean at all.

They’re grown in large circular tanks in a facility called Kuterra, built by the Namgis First Nation in 2013 for $10 million as a demonstration project to prove that a land-based aquaculture industry is possible in B.C.

More than 10 years in, the project is still going, with some changes. The facility used to produce salmon but has found it’s easier to produce trout, said Chief Don Svanvik of the Namgis First Nation.

“It’s incredible. It’s a big investment,” Svanvik said in an interview in Port McNeill. “But it’s happening. If it was easy, everybody would be doing it.”

A study commissioned by the B.C. government in 2021 found that the experience of Kuterra may be hard to replicate, warning of high capital costs, difficulty obtaining power, and regulatory uncertainty.

“The results are not promising,” said the report, by Counterpoint Consulting, saying the estimated rate of return is too low at 8.7 per cent for a large farm and 5.8 per cent for a medium-sized farm.

“Those rates of return are far too low to attract the investment required to incentivize the development of a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) salmon farming industry in British Columbia,” the report said.

“We have concluded from our research and analysis that RAS development in BC is possible, but at smaller scales and not in isolation from the larger aquaculture sector currently operating in BC,” the report said.

Tony Allard, a businessman who is the chair of the environmental group Wild First, admits land-based farms can be “capital-intensive.”

But he said there are other advantages, pointing to another land-based farm near Tokyo, which he said saves on transportation costs because it’s right next to its market.

Allard said that there is investor interest in making these work, especially if the open net pen farming is shut down.

“It has proved the concept. It’s grown fish, and it’s sold them at a premium,” he said in an interview.

“And that’s where the growth of this industry is. So, keep the ban, no half-measures, and let’s grow this industry safely, sustainably, on land,” he said.

Imports filling the gaps

Canadian consumers may not be waiting around as foreign fish farms have rushed in to fill the gaps left by shuttered West Coast fish farms.

One major grocery chain, Loblaws, told CTV News in a statement that it sources salmon from a variety of Canadian and international suppliers, and prices vary based on a number of factors.

“Reduced domestic supply in recent years has meant we are relying more on imported salmon; however, Canadian salmon remains an important part of our assortment, and we will continue to source domestically where supply and market conditions allow,” the statement said.

In 2016, Canada imported about $90.5 million in fish categories including Atlantic salmon, according to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada and Statistics Canada. That number quadrupled to $356 million in 2025.

It was a similar surge from Norway, whose exports to Canada rose from $34 million to $158 million.

And Iceland’s exports surged 22 times, from $0.8 million to $20 million in the same time period.

“I think that’s a challenge for Canadians to wake up and turn around and look and say, is this something that we want? Do we want to import fish?” asked Richard Opala, a regulatory affairs manager at Mowi Canada West.

“Well, we can grow it here. Do we want to support jobs in other countries when we don’t have them here?” he said.

But critics of the fish farm industry say that Canadian wild stocks could be better protected if Canadians order from farms in ecosystems without competing salmon.

“The stakes are higher here than they are in Norway, where there are no longer any commercial fisheries,” said Kristi Miller, a scientist who used to work with the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans.

“It’s different here in British Columbia, because we still have large, abundant populations of wild fish. We still have commercial fisheries. We still have recreational fisheries, we still have Indigenous fisheries,” she said.

Coastal community worries

Some First Nations groups are concerned enough about the potential impact of salmon farms they are calling for the eviction of remaining salmon farms near Port Hardy.

“What wild salmon mean to First Nations all across the province is beyond valuation. It contributes to food security across the province. It is the basis of our culture and traditions. And is not an item we wish to see impacted while others make profits,” said Bob Chamberlin, chair of the First Nations Wild Salmon Alliance, at a news conference this month on Parliament Hill.

In Port Hardy, on northern Vancouver Island, Mayor Patricia Corbett-Labatt is concerned about what losing the remaining salmon farms would mean for her community.

“We are a fishing, logging, mining community. We’re resource based,” she said in an interview.

She said she is concerned about what would happen to the jobs, and by extension the community, if more farms are shut down.

“It would be very similar to when the mine closed here and there was a huge depression,” she said.

Over in the Queen Charlotte Strait, Guitard from Mowi takes a scoop of pellets and tosses it into an open pen. The fish respond by jumping.

She said she’s worried about what may be in store in 2029, when the ban is set to take effect, but is hopeful she can stay in her home in Campbell River.

“It’s awful, honestly. I’ve been here for six years. I have established a whole community, I have friends, it’s a lifestyle that I would love to live, but it really does rely solely on this industry continuing here.”

items.description: Bank of America has been fined US$1.21 billion by the U.S. government for what it called widespread failures to properly police potential money laundering and other illicit activity at the nation’s second-largest bank.

items._ogDesc: Bank of America has been fined US$1.21 billion by the U.S. government for what it called widespread failures to properly police potential money laundering and other illicit activity at the nation’s second-largest bank.
items.body:
Bank of America has been fined US$1.21 billion by the U.S. government for what it called widespread failures to properly police potential money laundering and other illicit activity at the nation’s second-largest bank.

The U.S. Treasury Department said the fine, the third-largest in department history, is due to the bank’s failure to report over US$5 billion in suspicious activity to the government, including US$1 billion in activity that posed national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks.

“Financial institutions are on the front lines of protecting our economic and national security,” said U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks.”

The Treasury said the bank “prioritized its revenues” in building compliance programs, and overly relied on inquiries from outside parties like law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls.

“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” said a Bank of America spokesperson in a statement. “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators.”

The spokesperson added that the bank’s third-quarter results due for release on Wednesday will include a non-tax-deductible charge of US$1.2 billion, which will reduce quarterly net income by approximately 17 cents a share. Shares were down 1.8 per cent in after-hours trading.

As part of the fine, the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency levied a US$750 million civil penalty against the lender, the largest ever for the regulator, citing failures to address shortcomings in its anti-money laundering programs that were identified as part of a 2024 cease-and-desist order from the watchdog.

The regulator said the bank’s compliance program was “deficient and ineffective,” and its transaction monitoring system caused the bank to delay in filing suspicious activity reports on billions of dollars of transactions.

In addition, the bank paid an US$11.6 million fine to the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control for over 400 apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs. The Treasury said the bank mistakenly processed millions of dollars in payments that violated sanctions programs targeting countries including Russia and Iran.

The fine comes days after American Express was also hit with a $350 million penalty for similar anti-money laundering shortcomings.

Ismail Shakil and Pete Schroeder, Reuters

items.title: TC Energy completes Indigenous investment deal in Coastal GasLink
items.description: A group representing five First Nations says it has invested $65.3 million for an interest in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, set for a big expansion.

items._ogDesc: A group representing five First Nations says it has invested $65.3 million for an interest in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, set for a big expansion.
items.body:
CALGARY — A group representing five First Nations says it has invested $65.3 million for an interest in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, which brings natural gas from northeastern B.C. to the LNG Canada plant in Kitimat — and is set for a big expansion.

FN CGL Pipeline Ltd. Partnership said in a news release Tuesday that members are putting up their own funds.

“Our Nations are making this investment with their own capital. No government loan guarantees, no borrowed money,” said Chief Harley Chingee of McLeod Lake Indian Band.

“It was a deliberate choice, the best way to secure maximum benefits from what we believe to be a sound commercial investment. The returns will now belong entirely to the communities, as will decisions as to how they are used.”

Other members of the group are the Haisla Nation, Halfway River First Nation, Saulteau First Nations and West Moberly First Nations.

“This investment framework recognizes the importance of partnership, financial certainty and shared prosperity, while supporting our communities’ ability to make decisions about our own economic future,” Chief Roland Willson of West Moberly First Nations said.

TC Energy chief executive François Poirier congratulated the First Nations on completing the deal.

“This transaction reflects years of collaboration, leadership and determination by the Nations involved to create a long-term economic opportunity for their communities.”

Coastal GasLink runs 670 kilometres from northeastern B.C. to Kitimat, B.C., with a capacity of 2.1 billion cubic feet per day. It is operated by TC Energy Corp.

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

Under the deal, FN CGL and TC Energy collectively now hold an indirect 35 per cent interest in the pipeline through a TC subsidiary. The remaining 65 per cent is held by KKR Co. and Alberta Investment Management Corp. on behalf of certain clients.

“The structure provides stable cash flows without typical equity volatility, helping support long-term planning and managing of community priorities,” a spokesperson for TC Energy said in an emailed statement.

“It provides long-term predictable distributions, providing stable investment income while reducing risks associated with direct ownership.”

Tuesday’s deal is the first of two planned Indigenous investment transactions related to Coastal GasLink. TC Energy says a second transaction with another First Nations entity is expected to close in the fourth quarter of this year.

In 2022, TC Energy announced the signing of option agreements to sell a 10 per cent equity interest in the pipeline to Indigenous communities across the project corridor.

The company recently announced plans to double the existing capacity of the Coastal GasLink pipeline by adding new compressor stations and upgrading facilities.

For the second phase of the pipeline, LNG Canada — owned by Shell Canada and four Asian partners — is leading construction, limiting the Coastal GasLink owners’ spending and cost and schedule risk. The Coastal GasLink partners remain owners.

Construction is to begin in early 2027 and the expansion is set to come into service in the early 2030s.

The decision came after LNG Canada announced a final greenlight for the Phase 2 expansion of its facility, which enables natural gas chilled into a liquid state to be shipped across the Pacific. The first phase started up in the summer of 2025.

Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

items.body:
Lightspeed Commerce Inc. says 250 roles will be impacted as the company lays off staff and opts to not fill some vacancies.

The Montreal-based software business says the cuts are meant to simplify its operations and create room to reinvest in customer growth and product innovations.

Spokesperson Stéphanie Princivil did not answer questions about what areas of the company the layoffs and removal of vacancies targeted but said in an email that Lightspeed will provide more information when it reports quarterly earnings next month.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Lightspeed has made several staffing cuts over the last few years as Dax Dasilva, Lightspeed’s founder and chief executive, returned to the top job.

In hopes of creating more shareholder value, the company also conducted a strategic review, but it concluded last year with no go-private transaction.

Instead, the company opted to double down on its North American retail and European hospitality divisions and sell Upserve, a business it owned which offered restaurant management tools.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: The Ottawa-based defence company Dominion Dynamics is partnering with Ukrainian robotics company Tencore to start building its ground-based drone vehicles in Canada as early as next year.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The Ottawa-based defence company Dominion Dynamics is partnering with Ukrainian robotics company Tencore to start building its ground-based drone vehicles in Canada as early as next year.

The two companies signed a memorandum of understanding at a defence conference in Washington, D.C., today which outlines their plans to manufacture Tencore’s Termit drone in Canada and install Dominion’s software in the vehicles.

The Termit drone, which runs on treads and looks almost like a miniature tank, has been deployed to Ukraine’s front lines for operations that would be hazardous for humans, such as resupply missions and mine-laying.

The federal government has been pushing for joint production of drones by Canadian companies and Ukraine’s battle-tested defence industry.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in Calgary last month and signed a joint declaration on defence production.

Dominion is also independently developing its own autonomous collaborative platform: drones guided by humans that fly alongside fighter jets, such as F-35s or Gripen fighters.

items.title: Affordability remains a drag – but CEO says Canadians still aspire to own a home
items.description: Despite a challenging housing market outlook RE/MAX Canada’s Kottick says Canadians still want to buy, and are willing to compromise to do so
items.content: <p>Despite a challenging housing market outlook RE/MAX Canada’s Kottick says Canadians still want to buy, and are willing to compromise to do so</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639275023114611598.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Despite a challenging housing market outlook RE/MAX Canada’s Kottick says Canadians still want to buy, and are willing to compromise to do so
items.body:
Tariffs, economic uncertainty and affordability challenges may be hurting the national housing market – but Canadians are still clinging to the dream of homeownership despite those hurdles, according to RE/MAX Canada’s president.

The real estate giant’s latest housing market outlook, released last week, showed 65% of hopeful buyers surveyed are prepared to compromise in their efforts to own a home, including through relocation and cutting back on discretionary spending.

And Don Kottick, who’s helmed the organization as president since last year, told Canadian Mortgage Professional that the poll suggests homeownership appetite is still strong even with a sluggish market and challenging economic environment.

“Homeownership is still near and dear to the hearts of pretty much most Canadians,” he said. “Regardless of market conditions, regardless of headwinds, homeownership is still tied to who we are as Canadians.”

Widespread return to the city unlikely, says Kottick

Home affordability has improved modestly across many markets this year, although rising interest rates are eroding some of those gains. Some executives say the only solution to unlock a healthier market is for prices to drop even further.

But Kottick sees potential buyers who are on the verge of being able to afford a home taking pragmatic steps to get a purchase over the line.

“People are willing to sit a little longer in traffic to get that home that really appeals to their wants and their needs,” he said. “If they can get that bigger home [for less], they get better quality of life.”

The COVID-19 pandemic and the onset of a remote-working revolution pushed scores of buyers out of cramped apartments in big cities and toward more rural, spacious housing.

A hot topic of debate in the real estate sector since then is whether a ramping-up of return-to-office efforts could see buyers turn their attention back to cities and away from suburban and rural areas, but Kottick isn’t convinced.

“It’s not happening like, flip a switch and everybody’s back. It’s something that’s kind of a work in progress,” he said. “There’s a lot of discussion on it, a lot of talk on it – and probably a lot of resistance to it.”

Regional picture varies, but much will depend on BoC for 2027

About 32% of housing markets analyzed by RE/MAX’s latest report now sit in buyer’s market territory, a jump from 15.2% last year, as softer conditions emerge in many parts of the country.

Home sales were down in 81% of markets analyzed, the survey said. But while the outlook for the national market is cloudy, it’s often highlighted that the regional picture can vary widely from one province or city to the next – and prices actually increased in 56% of markets.

Some regional markets are still showing notable strength, Kottick said, with Northern Ontario cities including Sudbury, Thunder Bay, Kenora and Sault Ste. Marie seeing sellers’ market conditions holding.

Saskatoon and St. John’s, Newfoundland, meanwhile, are also bucking the broader national trend. “We still have these pockets that are really resilient, really strong,” Kottick said. “The recovery is definitely slower in some of the major markets where there’s been more price appreciation over time.”

Still, it goes without saying that the continuing trade war with the US and inflation fears as a result of the US-Iran war are keeping a lid on homebuying demand.

Rising oil prices have sent inflation expectations soaring in recent weeks, with chances of at least one Bank of Canada rate hike in the coming months also reportedly growing.

The central bank is scheduled to make its next decision at the end of this month, although at least one top economist has questioned the need for rate hikes – especially with the economy continuing to weaken.  

Kottick said the trajectory into next year will depend on those factors, and whether there’s good news ahead on the economic front.

“If we can get the macro headwinds resolved, we very well could see the market really pick up in 2027,” he said.

items.description: Mortgage brokers will gather at Rebel Toronto on November 25 for the program’s 20th-anniversary gala
items.content: <p>Mortgage brokers will gather at Rebel Toronto on November 25 for the program’s 20th-anniversary gala</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639275163379725593.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Mortgage brokers will gather at Rebel Toronto on November 25 for the program’s 20th-anniversary gala
items.body:
Canada’s mortgage brokers will gather at Rebel Toronto on Wednesday, November 25, for the 20th Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs), the national recognition program presented by Canadian Mortgage Professional (CMP).

The shortlist is already set. In September, CMP named its 2026 excellence awardees, the final shortlisted candidates across 23 competitive categories. That makes the gala the night the results go public, and much of the broker channel’s networking happens there too. 

The business case for mortgage brokers

1. A milestone edition two decades in the making

The 2026 gala marks 20 years of the program recognizing the professionals, firms and leaders moving the Canadian mortgage industry forward. An event that has lasted two decades has outlived several rate cycles. That longevity is the reason a CMA carries weight with clients and lenders. 

2. The shortlist resolves live

Readers can already review the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards excellence awardees. Among them in Eastern Canada are Anthony Di Feo of Multi-Prêts Mortgages, Nicole Farrugia of Vine Group and Paul Meredith of PMT Mortgage Corp.

Winners in all 26 categories will be revealed at the gala, so attendees see the results first. 

3. The results are independently judged

The outcome is not decided by popularity. Winners are chosen through a points system that tallies the judging panel’s votes, and the excellence awardee with the highest score in each category takes the award.

CMP has profiled the five independent judges scoring this year’s submissions. Their backgrounds span academic research, regulatory law, federal housing policy and executive leadership in Canadian mortgage and finance.

The panel includes Andrey Pavlov, professor of finance at Simon Fraser University’s Beedie School of Business in Vancouver. 

4. A benchmark for your own 2027 plan

The judging criteria double as a business review. For broker categories, judges weigh loan volumes, year-over-year growth, lead generation, client retention, conversion rates and overall customer service.

Broker of the Year is awarded in three regions: Maritimes/Atlantic Canada, Eastern Canada and Western Canada. Only category winners advance to compete for the overall Canadian Broker of the Year title. 

5. Your lender partners in one room

The program recognizes business development managers (BDMs) and underwriters, not just brokers.

In the BDM categories, nominations coming directly from the broking community carry considerable weight.

The 2026 sponsors include CMI Canadian Mortgages Inc., Equitable Bank, Haventree Bank, MCAN Mortgage Corporation, RFA Mortgage Corporation and Real Property Solutions Inc.

With renewal volumes still elevated, a face-to-face conversation with a lender’s leadership team can be worth more than a dozen emails. 

6. The industry’s decision-makers, all in one place

The gala draws hundreds of leading mortgage professionals and senior executives from top organizations. Few other evenings put brokerage principals, network heads and lender executives in the same room. 

7. A preview of where the broker’s role is heading

Two categories are new this year: Mortgage Tech Innovator of the Year and The REMIC Award for Finfluencer of the Year.

The finfluencer category judges entrants partly on compliance awareness and adherence to Canadian regulatory and advertising guidelines for mortgage promotions. That is a signal of how digital advice is expected to mature. 

What to expect on the night

8. Recognition for the whole team

Brokerage and team categories are split at 25 employees, so smaller shops compete with peers of a similar size.

The evening also includes the Haventree Bank Award for Lifetime Achievement, the program’s highest honour, which has no finalists and is announced only at the ceremony. 

9. Recognition that pays off after the gala

Past winners say the award works long after the trophy is handed out. “Developers and investors need confidence in their advisor from day one,” said Akshay Gupta, a commercial real estate mortgage agent at Foundry Mortgage Capital Corp. in Toronto and the 2025 Young Achiever of the Year.

Kyle Benzies of DLC AIMI Collective Mortgage Group put it more directly: “Being a part of this, it’ll actually change the trajectory of my business.”

10. A well-run evening

The cocktail reception will run from 6 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. It will be followed by the awards ceremony and seated dinner until 10:30 p.m., then a post-awards celebration. The host is broadcaster Sonia Mangat, who appears on eTalk and CP24 Breakfast.

Entertainment will come from the five-piece band Soulfire and a Frank Sinatra tribute by Jesse Posa. 

Registration is open at canadianmortgageawards.com/register-now.

The post Canada’s Housing Crash Rivals US In 2008, But The Pain Is Hidden: BMO appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canada’s home prices fell more than 20%, but BMO says population growth may have masked the economic pain of the housing crash.
items.body:
Canada’s housing crash is close to rivalling the early 2000s crash in the US. In contrast, Canada seems relatively unscathed, despite being a smaller economy that’s more dependent on housing. BMO’s chief economist notes the country is better positioned to avoid a financial crisis, but its pain avoidance is partly an illusion—hidden by Canada’s aggressive use of immigration.

Canadian Home Prices Are Following The US Housing Crash

Source: BMO Capital Markets; CREA.

The Canadian housing correction is following the same trajectory as the U.S., but with a different outcome. Home prices in Canada have dropped 20.5% from the early-2022 peak, compared with 26% during the U.S. bust. However, Canada avoided a comparable economic collapse—its real GDP grew at an annualized pace of 1.7% over the four years since prices started falling. That’s only slightly below the 2.0% average for this century, which is remarkable considering the country’s housing-dependent economy.

“This is arguably the most significant home price correction ever for Canada, and yet the economy has managed to avoid serious collateral damage from the deep decline,” explains BMO Chief Economist Douglas Porter.

He notes Canada has seen only one “traditional” recession in the past 35 years. That was the Global Financial Crisis, with 2020 being a very different policy-induced shutdown. He clarifies, “… it’s not as if recessions never happen, they are now just extremely rare events, and it takes a near cataclysm to cause a full-scale downturn.”

How? There’s some clear factors that helped mitigate the worst of the fallout—at least on the surface.

Stronger Borrowers And Rate Cuts Helped Contain The Fallout

The bank sees the brief period of peak home prices as one of the key differentiators. Porter notes prices surged 50% over the final two years, containing the damage to a relatively small pool. The correction is also largely contained in two provinces, leaving prices relatively unscathed for almost half the country. A substantial wealth cushion also helps limit spending cutbacks, while an aging population increasingly supports consumption through non-employment income such as pensions. In fact, seniors (aged 65+) represented over 1 in 5 (22.4%) dollars of consumption in 2025.

Source: BMO; Haver Analytics; Statistics Canada.

The bank also notes that the finances were stronger. Mortgage qualification hurdles, like the stress test, helped minimize the volume of overextended borrowers. Rate cuts began less than a year after rates peaked, softening the normalization shock. Overall, the headline data reveals an economy that’s darn near invincible.

Skeptical that a housing-based economy could survive a US-style housing correction with so little damage? There’s a good reason—the apparent escape may have been partly an illusion, according to Porter.

Canada Avoided A Financial Crisis, But It Didn’t Avoid The Pain

Porter believes Canada avoided the financial crisis, but avoiding the pain is partly an “illusion.” The population grew at an annualized pace of 2.8% over two years to early 2024, generally faster than GDP averaged. This helped to offset—possibly more than offset—any pullback in GDP. The economy grew, but the population grew faster—meaning less economic output per person, despite headline gains.

Source: BMO; Haver Analytics; Statistics Canada.

Measured per person, real GDP per capita fell in four of five quarters during the 2022-23 stretch, falling more than 2% peak-to-trough. Unemployment also climbed more than 2 percentage points over that period, a rare combination. Porter says this has only occurred a handful of times in the past 60 years—and only during official recessions.

Source: BMO; Haver Analytics; Statistics Canada.

“In other words, some of Canada’s Housing Houdini may have in fact been an illusion, not unlike the original act,” says Porter.

items.title: Canada’s asking rents fall for 24 straight months
items.description: September data marks two years of declines, with condo rents falling 7.8% year-over-year
items.content: <p>September data marks two years of declines, with condo rents falling 7.8% year-over-year</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639275116349329493.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: September data marks two years of declines, with condo rents falling 7.8% year-over-year
items.body:
Canada’s rental market has recorded 24 consecutive months of annual price declines, the longest downturn in recent histor. Average asking rents fell 4.2% year-over-year in September to $2,034, according to the National Rent Report from Rentals.ca and Urbanation.

The reading leaves asking rents 9.2% below their May 2024 peak of $2,202 and 7.3% lower on a cumulative two-year basis.

Supply driving the correction

Supply, not weakening demand, is the primary force behind the prolonged downturn, according to Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand.

“Our research shows supply has been the main driver of this correction, and in key markets like Toronto and Vancouver, new supply is moving past its peak,” Hildebrand said.

“Rents in both cities have trended higher over the past six months, and annual declines have narrowed significantly as renters come off the sidelines. Where Toronto and Vancouver go, the rest of the country follows.”

The data showed divergence by property type. Purpose-built apartments recorded the smallest annual decline, falling 2.7% to $2,036.

Condominium apartments took the steepest hit, down 7.8% to $2,052, led by a 9.6% drop in studio condo rents.

Secondary market units such as houses and townhomes fell 7.4% year-over-year to $2,016.

Further condo price declines may still be needed before the segment recovers, a challenge that is complicating client conversations and appraisal conditions in volatile urban segments.

Christine Xu, founder of Money Broker Canada and a 26-year industry veteran, put the situation plainly at MortgageFest Canada 2026.

“A lot of those people are racing masters — they invest in a whole bunch of pre-construction condos and they are being hit the most,” she said.

“We see bankruptcy all over the place.”

Provincial picture and the affordability outlook

The correction has been uneven across provinces. Ontario saw asking rents fall 4.8% year-over-year, British Columbia 2.9%, Alberta 2.6%, and Quebec 1.7%. Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia each posted 1.4% gains.

On a per-square-foot basis, average rents across Canada’s six largest markets came in at $2.48 in September 2026, down 1.5% from September 2025.

Separate figures from Statistics Canada cited in the report show average weekly earnings have risen 19.4% over the past five years, a measure the report used to illustrate a gradual improvement in rental affordability.

However, falling asking rents have not resolved Canada’s rental affordability crisis, with renter budgets remaining deeply misaligned with market pricing in most major cities.

A structural signal worth watching: Canada’s rental vacancy rate dipped for the first time in two years in Q2, a shift that Yardi’s multifamily data attributed to supply pipelines approaching their ceiling.

The Rentals.ca and Urbanation report identified peaking construction inventories, modest revised population growth, and limited tariff exposure in both cities’ labour markets as conditions that could support a return to positive rent growth in Toronto and Vancouver.

That inflection, the report concluded, may be closer than two years of uninterrupted declines suggest.

items.title: Mortgage brokers are losing past clients between renewals
items.description: Past-client referrals are slipping, and the fix starts long before renewal day
items.content: <p>Past-client referrals are slipping, and the fix starts long before renewal day</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639275090700400938.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Past-client referrals are slipping, and the fix starts long before renewal day
items.body:
Canadian mortgage brokers are losing ground with past clients. Speakers at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September said the damage happens in the quiet years between mortgage renewals.

The share of brokers naming past clients as their strongest referral source fell to 44.66% in 2026 from 56.28% a year earlier, according to Canadian Mortgage Professional’s 20th annual Brokers on Lenders survey of 459 brokers.

Realtor referrals rose to a three-year high of 34.86% over the same period, which the survey linked to renewal anxiety.

Why do mortgage brokers lose clients between renewals?

Dan MacDonald, chief executive of Ownwell, a broker engagement platform based in Vancouver, said most homeowners hear little of substance once a deal funds.

“What we call the unmonitored market in between renewals. The banks aren’t really providing much value to their clients, nor are most mortgage brokers. So in those years between closing and their next renewal, maybe they’re getting a happy birthday email or a list of Thanksgiving recipes. They get forgotten,” he said.

“We see in our data about 1 in 10 existing mortgage holders experiences a mortgage-related event every year outside of their normal cycle. So that’s the opportunity for brokers in this market.”

The cost of ignoring that window is rising. Renewing borrowers saw their monthly payments climb by an average of $375, according to Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation’s (CMHC) 2026 Mortgage Consumer Survey. That kind of pressure rarely waits for a maturity date.

Working the book before the banks do

Lenders are not waiting. Bank executives at the event described bank retention teams reaching renewing clients earlier. Elena Robinson, vice-president of residential sales at First National Financial LP, urged brokers to plan at least a year ahead.

“I think for brokers, make sure that you own the client before someone else has the opportunity to do so,” Robinson said.

Sarita Free, a mortgage agent with Mortgage Powered Financial Group in Norfolk County, Ontario, framed the same point as a daily discipline.

“Work your book. I know you’ve probably heard that from other agents, but work your book. Stay in contact with your clients. Look for opportunities where their rate might be high. Know your clients,” she said.

Tracy Valko, founder of AIMI Mortgage Collective, said the role itself has to change.

“As an industry, we got away from where it was about transactions and how many deals you did. Now it’s about focusing on that financial plan and strategy for that client, building that long-term financial relationship. So you look like a true expert and not just a rate agent,” Valko said.

The stakes are rising. The share of Canadians who obtained their mortgage through a broker climbed to 38% in 2026, according to Mortgage Professionals Canada. That means more clients sitting in broker books, years from their next maturity date.

items.title: New Brunswick gets $219 million loan from Ottawa for hydroelectric dam repair work
items.description: The federal government is spending nearly $270 million to help New Brunswick modernize a pair of energy facilities that officials say are key to Ottawa’s plan to double the capacity of  Canada’s electrical grid by 2050.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The intake structure, powerhouse and main spillway of the Mactaquac generating station are shown on Tuesday, Dec.20, 2016. THE CANADIAN PRESS/James West]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">James West</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The federal government is spending nearly $270 million to help New Brunswick modernize a pair of energy facilities that officials say are key to Ottawa’s plan to double the capacity of  Canada’s electrical grid by 2050.
items.body:
MACTAQUAC — The federal government is investing nearly $270 million in loans and grants to help New Brunswick modernize energy facilities that officials say are key to Ottawa’s plan to double the capacity of Canada’s electrical grid by 2050.

The bulk of the money is a $219-million loan from the Canada Infrastructure Bank to extend the life of the province’s largest hydroelectric dam, located west of Fredericton on the Saint John River.

The province will also receive a $50-million grant to upgrade its Salisbury Terminal near Moncton, which officials say is key to managing the flow of electricity across the provincial grid.

Federal Energy Minister Tim Hodgson made the announcements Tuesday during a news conference in front of the massive Mactaquac Dam.

“New Brunswick is critical to this plan and so are today’s investments,” he said. “Together, these two projects will strengthen New Brunswick’s electricity system while creating jobs, attracting investment, supporting affordability, and lowering emissions.”

New Brunswick’s Crown-owned electric utility is preparing the 672-megawatt Mactaquac Generation Station for a multibillion-dollar overhaul aimed at extending its operational life to 2068.

The new funding will pay for technical studies, regulatory reviews, First Nations engagement and planning for the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project, according to Natural Resources Canada.

In 2016, NB Power agreed to a plan in 2016 to spend up to $3.6 billion to prolong the life of the dam, which would have otherwise been decommissioned by 2030 due to concrete swelling.

The new funding will support technical studies, regulatory reviews, First Nations engagement and planning for the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project, according to Natural Resources Canada.

On Tuesday, NB Power CEO Lori Clark said the total cost for the project is now expected to be close to $9 billion.

Hodgson would not commit the federal Liberal government to spending more on the dam, noting that electricity generation is within provincial jurisdiction.

However, he said the federal government will need to help provinces and territories keep costs low as they work to meet federal clean energy regulations that call for a net-zero electricity grid by 2050.

“In the budget coming up, you will see a number of initiatives we are working on to work ... with provinces and territories to help them realize the growth that they need in an affordable way,” the minister told reporters.

“This is clearly an indication that we understand how important it is for our prosperity to grow our electricity generating capabilities and we understand that the federal government needs to do its part in helping to make that affordable.”

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt said the Mactaquac Generating Station is important to the entire Maritime region.

In the event of a system-wide blackout, the dam can start generating electricity without relying on an external power supply, making the largest so-called “black-start” facility in the region.

“We often call it the battery of the Maritimes,” said Holt. “Having this kind of renewable energy that we can turn on and off is critical, not only to our province, but to our neighbours in Prince Edward Island and in Nova Scotia and beyond.”

The dam supplies 30 per cent of the province’s renewable energy requirements and 20 per cent of its overall electricity demand, officials said.

The investments come as NB Power is looking for ways to fix ageing infrastructure without imposing massive rate hikes on its customers.

Since the 1980s, concrete portions of the the dam have been affected by a chemical process called alkali-aggregate reaction. The reaction causes concrete to swell and crack, requiring substantial repairs and maintenance.

Just last week, NB Power applied to the provincial regulator to raise rates by 17.4 per cent over the next three years as it plans to spend $4 billion on maintaining the provincial grid.

Some of that money will be used to transition the province’s only remaining coal-fired generating plant to a facility that burns wood pellets to generate electricity.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

items.title: Bond yield warning from IMF puts Canada’s fixed rates on notice
items.description: Global bond pressure the IMF flagged is already landing on Canadian mortgage renewals
items.content: <p>Global bond pressure the IMF flagged is already landing on Canadian mortgage renewals</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639275044634571431.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Global bond pressure the IMF flagged is already landing on Canadian mortgage renewals
items.body:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned on October 13 that a sharper rise in government bond yields ranks among the most plausible near-term threats to global financial stability, a risk Canadian mortgage borrowers are already absorbing at renewal.

In its October 2026 Global Financial Stability Report, released in Bangkok during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, the fund said sovereign yields have climbed on higher energy prices and rising term premiums, the extra return investors demand for holding longer-dated debt. Those premiums now sit at the upper end of historical ranges, particularly in advanced economies, the report said.

“The market is concerned about absorption potential of the huge issuance that is coming from the sovereigns and increasingly also from the private sector, at the time that central banks are shrinking their balances, and we have to rely more on price-sensitive investors,” Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director in the IMF’s Monetary and Capital Markets Department, told reporters.

Global bond pressure is reaching Canadian fixed mortgage rates

Canada has not been spared. The five-year Government of Canada bond yield, the benchmark lenders use to price five-year fixed mortgages, closed at 3.60% on October 2, up from 3.35% on September 1, according to Bank of Canada data. 

Lenders have followed the market. Since early September, all of the Big Six banks have raised at least some fixed rates, with cumulative increases of roughly 10 to 50 basis points across two- to five-year terms. BMO lifted its standard five-year fixed rate to 5.14% on October 7.

That repricing has come while the Bank of Canada holds its overnight rate at 2.25%, extending pressure that began with an oil-fuelled bond selloff that pushed Canada’s 10-year yield to 3.9% in September.

“For most households out there, it simply doesn’t matter why bond yields are rising. It matters that they are,” RBC economist Claire Fan said on the bank’s The 10-Minute Take podcast.

Sabeena Bubber, a mortgage broker at Xeva Mortgage, said at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September that banks are steering borrowers on headline rate alone.

“Now more than ever it’s so important for people to use a mortgage broker rather than their bank, because the banks are specifically just focusing on rates. As we head into a turbulent time where potentially we will see an increase in rates, the banks are putting clients in, say, a variable rate, which may not be the best option for that client – just because it has a three in front of it,” Bubber said.

The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) says frontier AI is among the fastest-growing threats facing lenders, warning that advanced models can help adversaries identify and exploit vulnerabilities at greater speed and scale. https://t.co/B9plArK6ju — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 12, 2026

What the IMF warning means for mortgage renewals

The report singled out household exposure. It urged authorities to monitor debt-servicing burdens “particularly in jurisdictions where mortgage payments are sensitive to interest rate fluctuations,” and said limits on loan-to-value or debt-service-to-income ratios can curb excessive household leverage.

The IMF also warned that a renewed surge in energy prices could reignite inflation, force tighter monetary policy and lift yields abruptly through term-premium shocks.

Tracy Valko, founder of AIMI Mortgage Collective, told the MortgageFest audience that brokers need to understand those forces.

“There’s a lot of global tensions right now that are affecting our market. What’s affecting bond yields? What affects fixed rates? Agents and brokers should know that. We as mortgage agents and brokers should never predict, but one thing we should do is make sure that we understand the knowledge so we can future-prepare homeowners for what could be coming down the pipeline,” Valko said.

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres (DLC), expects the Bank of Canada to raise rates by late 2026 or the first half of 2027. She explained why she believes mortgage rates aren’t falling anytime soon.

“We have to expect higher interest rates, which also means that fixed-rate mortgages are very attractive now,” she said.

Not everyone sees renewals as a flashpoint. Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, said at MortgageFest that the industry’s preparation has blunted the risk.

“We’re in normal rates today. We’re not in obscenely high rates. So I think the renewal cliff doesn’t exist to the extreme, but it’s something we need to be aware of,” Armstrong said.

items.title: How Olivia Chow And Brad Bradford Plan To Address Toronto’s Housing Woes
items.description:
As the October 26 Toronto mayoral election approaches, the city’s housing and affordability crisis remains one of the most pressing issues among voters, and for good reason.

Fewer than 1 in 6 Torontonians can afford to buy a home in the city, minimum wage workers have to work 145 hours per month to afford the average asking rent for a one-bedroom apartment, and while the city pledged to facilitate 285,000 new homes by 2031 in 2022, it’s only achieved 32% of that goal as of this August.

Toronto’s top mayoral candidates — Incumbent Mayor Olivia Chow, and former urban planner and City Councillor Brad Bradford — both say they can put a good dent in Toronto’s housing and affordability woes, but they differ on how to pull it off. Here’s how Bradford and Chow plan to tackle the housing file:

Olivia Chow

City-led affordable housing

Under Chow’s lead, housing has shifted out from under the domain of the private market toward a more public, city-led development model. Since Chow took office in 2023, 5,271 city-owned housing units have broken ground, including 1,680 affordable units. Her plan is to continue building affordable and rental units via her public development model, with a goal of delivering 65,000 rent-controlled homes by 2030. She also wants to encourage development through new incentive programs that cut fees for developers in exchange for affordable units.

Cutting red tape

Chow champions zoning reforms that allow for more missing middle housing, including as-of-right multiplexes, and fast tracking transit-oriented developments. She’s also working to streamline the development review process with pre-approved building plans and expanding the online application process with automated checks and submissions. Chow has said efforts like these have made Toronto 80% faster at approving new housing. She has also eliminated development charges (DCs) for projects up to six units, created an incentive program that eliminates DCs for purpose-built rental housing, and played a central role in securing the $1.5 billion tri-governmental deal to lower DCs by 40%-60% in June.

Protecting tenants

Chow has promised a $2.15-million bad landlord task force under RentSafeTO, if re-elected. The task force would use enforcement officers and lawyers to investigate reports of neglectful landlords and buildings in disrepair. Fines paid by landlords and RentSafeTO funds would pay for the initiative.

Expanding taxes

Chow says she backs increasing taxes on vacant and luxury homes to fund affordable housing and prevent speculation. It’s a stance she has been consistent on. In 2023, she created the luxury property tax and voted to increase the vacant homes tax from 1% to 3%.

Brad Bradford

Private development

Bradford disagrees with Chow’s public builder model for delivering affordable housing, favouring partnering with experienced non-profit and market builders who he believes can build housing faster and cheaper than the City has.

Cutting red tape

As the former Chair of the Planning and Housing Committee, Bradford brought forward the Housing Action Plan to legalize gentle density, update urban design rules like eliminating the angular plane, and speed up approvals. If elected, he promises to continue updating city guidelines and streamlining the development review process, in part by increasing the use of technology. Bradford has also long called for the dropping of DCs to get shovels in the ground faster. He put forward a motion to lower DCs by 25% last March, which was rejected by Chow, and voted in favour of slashing DCs by 40% or 50% this June.

Renter strategy

Bradford is proposing a three-part plan to help renters: “Keep your home. Cool your home. Build more homes.” He wants to keep the existing renoviction by-law, but improve its enforcement by implementing a public dashboard to keep track of licenses and investigations and provide more funding for enforcement. He also wants to ensure renters have at least one cool room in their house, without any rent hikes to pay for it. Finally, Bradford promises clearer rules and earlier funding for non-profit rental builders instead of one-off negotiations for each site.

No to taxation

Bradford is against raising taxes on vacant and luxury homes, and has said he wants to keep costs down for all Torontonians. If elected, Bradford also promises to eliminate Toronto's Municipal Land Transfer Tax for homes valued at or below $1.1 million.

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canada Lost 110,000 Jobs Over Two Months, Wiping Out 2026 Gains

The narrative of Canada’s resilient job market has flipped in just two months. Employment fell by roughly 70,000 jobs in September, totaling a drop of 110,000 since August. The two-month slump was so sharp that it wiped out any year-to-date gains, putting 2026 in the red. Bearing the brunt of the downturn are entrepreneurs, public workers, and young adults. This seems to be an increasingly common theme in recent years.

Canadian Rents Fall For 24th Month, Driven By Shrinking Unit Size

The average rent landlords are asking fell for a 24th straight month across Canada. The average fell to $2,034/month in September, 4.2% lower than last year and 9.2% below the May 2024 peak. A breakdown reveals the data is heavily skewed by region and size. The drop in Ontario was enough to eliminate the continued surge in provinces like Nova Scotia. At the same time, more than half of the national drop can be explained by shrinking apartment sizes.

Canadians Continue Migrating To Alberta and BC, Flee Ontario

Canada’s great internal migration shows over 110,000 residents moved to a new province in Q2 2026. The biggest winner continues to be Alberta’s net gain of 5,893 residents in Q2 2026, making it the top destination. Ontario was on the losing end, with 7,063 more residents leaving than it gained from other provinces. Holding onto the bottom of the list for years now suggests Ontario’s problems are now systemic.

Toronto Real Estate

Toronto Home Prices Plunge To 6-Year Low, 28% Below Peak

The price of a typical home across Greater Toronto fell 0.9% to $917,600 in September, and now sit 28.3% below March 2022’s peak. Last month saw the second-weakest sales volume for September in over 15 years. Active listings also came in at the second-highest volume over the same period. The weak demand balance leaves the region in a buyer’s market, where prices are expected to fall.

Vancouver Real Estate

Vancouver Home Prices Hit A 5-Year Low As Buyers Pull Back

The price of a typical home across Greater Vancouver slipped 0.6% to $1.08 million in September, 5.5% lower than last year. The drop came with an 8.2% drop in sales, leaving volumes at levels rarely seen outside of a recession. Inventory tightened slightly, but remains at one of the highest September volumes. The persistently weak demand and strong inventory have pushed prices to a 5-year low.

items.body:
After a quieter summer, more homes came onto the Fraser Valley market in September, but buyers remain cautious despite declining prices.

There were 2,818 new listings in the region in September, an 18.8 per cent increase from August, according to the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board’s September market report. But the total was 18.2 per cent lower than a year earlier.

Sales totalled 922 in September, down two per cent from August and 4.2 per cent compared from September 2025.

“As buyers remain cautious and sellers face greater pressure to attract attention, subdued demand continues to weigh on home prices across the Fraser Valley,” the board said.

Benchmark prices continued to decline across property types in the region. The benchmark price for a detached home stood at $1.3 million, down 1.5 per cent from August and 8.8 per cent year-over-year.

The benchmark price for an apartment fell 0.9 per cent month-over-month and 9.3 per cent year-over-year to $461,800. Townhouses had a benchmark price of $745,300, down 0.7 per cent from August and 6.2 per cent from September 2025.

“For buyers who are in a position to act, this represents a significant shift in affordability and may create an opportunity for some households to move into a different segment of the market,” said Ishaq Ismail, chair of the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board, in a statement Monday.

Langley and North Delta saw stronger performance than some other cities in the region. Langley had 226 sales in September, up 3.1 per cent from August and 4.1 per cent from a year earlier. New listings rose 20.7 per cent month-over-month to 583.

North Delta recorded 39 sales, a 34.4 per cent increase from August, although sales were down 4.8 per cent year-over-year. New listings increased 32.5 per cent month-over-month.

Surrey had 1,124 new listings in September, a 15.6 per cent decline from July and a 17.8 per cent decline from August 2025. Sales edged up 0.7 per cent compared with August 2025 to 404.

In Abbotsford, new listings rose 24.5 per cent from August to 365, while sales fell 21.5 per cent to 113. Compared with September 2025, new listings were down 15.7 per cent and sales declined 18.1 per cent.

Mission saw new listings jump 42.3 per cent month-over-month to 148, while sales fell 9.4 per cent to 48. Year over year, new listings declined 13.4 per cent and sales dropped 22.5 per cent.

“A succession of economic shocks have conspired to weigh on consumer confidence, keeping many buyers on the sidelines,” said Anthony Boone, interim CEO of the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board, in a statement.

“Despite lower prices and more choice, buyers remain cautious, and that is being reflected in the pace of sales.”

Across the Fraser Valley in September, condos took an average of 46 days to sell, while single-family detached homes took 45 days. Townhomes took an average of 38 days to sell.
